CausalChain: Hypoxia in HCC -> HIF-1α upregulation -> Increased ENTPD2 (and CD39/CD73) expression -> Enhanced conversion of extracellular ATP to AMP -> Elevated adenosine levels in TME -> Recruitment and activation of MDSCs -> Suppression of CTL activity -> Tumor immune evasion -> Inhibition of ENTPD2, CD39/CD73 and metabolic modulation -> Reduced adenosine accumulation -> Decreased MDSC infiltration -> Restoration of CTL function -> Enhanced efficacy of PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that in hypoxic hepatocellular carcinoma, a combinatorial inhibition of ENTPD2 and compensatory ectonucleotidases (CD39/CD73) will significantly reduce extracellular adenosine accumulation, leading to a marked decrease in the recruitment and activation of myeloid-derived suppressor cells. By simultaneously targeting key metabolic reprogramming pathways through selective modulation of AMPK-autophagy signaling, cytotoxic T lymphocyte function can be restored, thereby enhancing the antitumor efficacy of PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint blockade. This strategy will be rigorously evaluated using CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing to create precise knockouts and single-cell metabolomic and transcriptomic profiling to monitor both immunological and metabolic responses, ensuring that any compensatory shifts are accurately mapped and addressed.
Abstract: In hypoxic hepatocellular carcinoma, a dual-targeted therapeutic strategy that concurrently inhibits ENTPD2 and its compensatory ectonucleotidases (CD39/CD73) is proposed to precisely modulate adenosine levels in the tumor microenvironment. By using contemporary gene editing (CRISPR-Cas9) and single-cell multiomics (metabolomic and transcriptomic profiling), we aim to dissect the contribution of the adenosine-MDSC axis in immune suppression and explore whether targeted modulation of metabolic adaptations (via regulators of AMPK-autophagy) can further enhance cytotoxic T lymphocyte function. This refined approach is intended to overcome the redundancy in adenosine production pathways and potentiate the efficacy of PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint blockade in HCC, while also controlling for metabolic reprogramming that may impact tumor growth and immune evasion.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis focused solely on ENTPD2 inhibition to reduce adenosine-mediated MDSC recruitment, with a plan to monitor compensatory mechanisms. The revised hypothesis integrates the inhibition of additional ectonucleotidases (CD39/CD73) to directly address potential redundancies already established by HIF-driven pathways, as noted in current observations. Additionally, while the original acknowledged metabolic reprogramming (via AMPK-autophagy signaling) as a compensatory mechanism, the new hypothesis explicitly includes targeted metabolic modulation to enhance therapeutic efficacy. Each step of the original causal chain remains central—hypoxia drives HIF-1α upregulation leading to increased adenosine production, which recruits MDSCs to suppress CTLs. The revised strategy strengthens intervention points by integrating multi-target gene editing and single-cell multiomics to ensure that both immune suppression and metabolic shifts are comprehensively addressed, thereby enhancing the efficacy of PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint inhibition.
